Mode 3 depends on these asynchronous writes to keep legacy storage in sync, so this can silently drop legacy writes.       "body": "Update calls Storage.Update with the provided rest.UpdatedObjectInfo and then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update asynchronously. UpdatedObjectInfo can be request-scoped or one-use, and it may compute the new object from the old object in the store that calls it. Legacy storage may therefore fail, consume an already-consumed payload, or apply the update to a different legacy state, producing a different object than unified storage. For dual-write convergence, legacy should receive the already-updated object returned from Storage.Update, ideally through a wrapper or deep copy."

In mode 3, legacy storage may still contain a stale copy, and this code path will never clean it up. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. Skipping legacy deletion on NotFound can leave divergent legacy objects permanently."

If unified storage reports an error or has already removed the collection while legacy storage still contains objects, the legacy data will remain and the stores will diverge. Storage implementations commonly mutate the object during create, and legacy storage may also mutate it. Returning to the caller while a background goroutine continues to use or mutate the same object can cause data races and inconsistent objects. findings.title: Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the request context and may be canceled immediately
findings.body: In Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its context from the incoming request context. When the API request completes, that context is canceled, so the asynchronous legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection can be canceled before it finishes. Mode 3 depends on these asynchronous writes to keep legacy storage in sync, so this can silently drop legacy writes. Use a detached context for the asynchronous operation, preserving only logging/values, not request cancellation.

findings.title: Legacy update reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo after it was already used by unified storage
findings.body: Update calls Storage.Update with the provided rest.UpdatedObjectInfo and then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update asynchronously. UpdatedObjectInfo can be request-scoped or one-use, and it may compute the new object from the old object in the store that calls it. Legacy storage may therefore fail, consume an already-consumed payload, or apply the update to a different legacy state, producing a different object than unified storage. For dual-write convergence, legacy should receive the already-updated object returned from Storage.Update, ideally through a wrapper or deep copy.

findings.title: Delete does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns NotFound
findings.body: Delete returns immediately if Storage.Delete fails, including when the object is not found in unified storage. In mode 3, legacy storage may still contain a stale copy, and this code path will never clean it up. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. Skipping legacy deletion on NotFound can leave divergent legacy objects permanently.

findings.title: DeleteCollection does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns an error
findings.body: DeleteCollection returns immediately if Storage.DeleteCollection fails, so Legacy.DeleteCollection is not attempted. If unified storage reports an error or has already removed the collection while legacy storage still contains objects, the legacy data will remain and the stores will diverge. For mode 3 dual-write cleanup, legacy deletion should still be attempted where appropriate, especially when the unified store reports the collection is already absent.

findings.title: Async legacy create uses the original object without copying it
findings.body: Create passes the same runtime.Object pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create call that was passed to Storage.Create. Storage implementations commonly mutate the object during create, and legacy storage may also mutate it. Returning to the caller while a background goroutine continues to use or mutate the same object can cause data races and inconsistent objects. The object should be deep-copied before being handed to the asynchronous legacy writer.

findings.title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
findings.body: After a successful unified-storage delete, recordStorageDuration is called with name as the kind label instead of options.Kind. This corrupts the metric's kind dimension and can introduce high-cardinality labels because every object name becomes a separate metric label value. The call should use options.Kind, as in the other methods.

findings.title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, Create records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This reports a unified-storage failure under legacy-store metrics, making storage and legacy latency/error metrics incorrect. It should call recordStorageDuration.

findings.title: Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration
findings.body: When Storage.Update fails, Update records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This mislabels unified-storage update failures as legacy-store update failures. It should call recordStorageDuration.

findings.title: Legacy delete-collection duration is recorded as a storage duration
findings.body: In the asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with recordStorageDuration. This reports legacy-store delete-collection latency/errors under unified-storage metrics. It should call recordLegacyDuration.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched logger
findings.body: Delete builds log with name, kind, and method values, but then sets the context logger to d.Log instead of log. Downstream code that extracts the logger from ctx will miss the request-specific fields, making debugging harder. The context should be set with log.

findings.title: Every write starts an unbounded goroutine for legacy replication
findings.body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each start a new goroutine for the legacy write. There is no queue, worker pool, semaphore, or other backpressure mechanism. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, write traffic can create a large number of blocked goroutines, increasing memory use and potentially destabilizing the process.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for outstanding asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Destroy closes both Storage and Legacy immediately, but mode 3 may still have outstanding goroutines calling Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, or Legacy.DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can then operate on destroyed storage, causing errors or panics. The dual writer should track outstanding asynchronous writes and wait for them, or at least cancel and drain them, during Destroy.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
findings.body: The asynchronous legacy paths only record metrics when the legacy operation fails; they no longer log the error. Since mode 3 returns success to the client as soon as unified storage succeeds, legacy failures are otherwise invisible. This makes diagnosing divergence between unified and legacy storage difficult. Errors from asynchronous legacy writes should be logged, ideally with the object identity and operation.

findings.title: Unit tests do not synchronize with or verify asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Mode 3 methods start background goroutines, but the unit tests return immediately after calling Create, Delete, Update, or DeleteCollection. There is no WaitGroup, channel, or injectable executor to wait for the legacy call. Some tests set legacy mock expectations but never assert them, while Delete and DeleteCollection do not set legacy expectations at all, so background mock calls may occur after the test finishes or panic as unexpected calls. These tests do not reliably prove that legacy writes happen.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration test assumes immediate legacy consistency despite asynchronous writes
findings.body: The new mode 3 integration test runs the same playlist CRUD suite, which creates/updates/deletes objects through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy API. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous, so the legacy API may not yet reflect the change. Without polling/eventual-consistency waits, this test can be flaky and may fail or pass for timing reasons rather than correctness.
